title: Proverbs 4:20–27
context: The father renews his call to attend to his words and keep them in the heart, the wellspring of life. Guarding the heart shows itself in honest speech, a focused gaze, level paths, and steady refusal to swerve toward evil. Both traditions see shared ground in this emphasis on the inner life shaping outward conduct within the wisdom tradition.

verses.text: My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings.
verses.arminianNotes: My son, attend to my words and turn your ear to my sayings. Arminian readers see another call for attentive listening, showing that wisdom must be received repeatedly. The father’s persistence reflects how easily attention can drift.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the father renewing his appeal for careful attention. Wisdom requires an open ear. Both traditions see the repeated call to listen as characteristic of these opening chapters.

verses.text: Let them not depart from your eyes. Keep them in the center of your heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Do not let these words leave your sight; keep them in the center of your heart. Arminian readers see the need to keep wisdom close and internalized. Wisdom must shape the inner life, not remain external.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heart as the place where wisdom must dwell. Keeping words in view and heart shows complete devotion. Both traditions share this emphasis on inward reception.

verses.text: For they are life to those who find them, and health to their whole body.
verses.arminianNotes: These words are life to those who find them and health to their whole body. Arminian readers see wisdom bringing wholeness to the entire person. Finding wisdom involves seeking it and receiving it gladly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wisdom bringing life and health in a holistic sense. The promise reflects general benefits of wise living. Both traditions read this as typical fruit rather than an absolute guarantee of health.

verses.text: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.
verses.arminianNotes: Guard your heart diligently, for from it flows the wellspring of life. Arminian readers see the heart as the center of choices and desires, requiring careful vigilance. What flows from the heart shapes the whole of life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heart as the source of life’s direction, needing constant guarding. The verse underscores the inward roots of conduct. Both traditions see shared ground in the call to watch over the heart above all else.

verses.text: Put away from yourself a perverse mouth. Put corrupt lips far from you.
verses.arminianNotes: Put away a perverse mouth and corrupt lips. Arminian readers see speech as an expression of the heart that must be disciplined. Guarding the heart includes guarding words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see crooked speech as incompatible with a wise heart. The mouth reveals what is within. Both traditions see this as practical wisdom about the power of speech.

verses.text: Let your eyes look straight ahead. Fix your gaze directly before you.
verses.arminianNotes: Let your eyes look straight ahead and fix your gaze before you. Arminian readers see focus and resolve in following the wise path. Distraction can lead away from wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a fixed gaze as resistance to wandering after evil. Steady focus keeps a person on course. Both traditions see shared ground in this call to single-minded attention.

verses.text: Make the path of your feet level. Let all of your ways be established.
verses.arminianNotes: Make the path of your feet level and let your ways be established. Arminian readers see careful planning and attention to one’s steps. Wise choices create stability in life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see deliberate consideration of one’s ways leading to stability. Established paths reflect a settled, wise life. Both traditions see this as practical guidance for walking carefully.

verses.text: Don’t turn to the right hand nor to the left. Remove your foot from evil.
verses.arminianNotes: Do not turn to the right or left; remove your foot from evil. Arminian readers see steadfast commitment to the wise path. Turning from evil is a continual decision the son must make.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call to stay on the straight path without deviation. Removing the foot from evil completes the chapter’s exhortation. Both traditions see shared ground in this closing summons to faithful, upright living.
